## Why this question matters

- Operational models typically require **structured inputs** for resource-allocation decisions.
- Much consequential organizational information is **unstructured**: clinical notes, incident reports, case descriptions, and service records.
- LLMs can convert those narratives into assessments that enter decision models.
- Yet an accurate assessment need not yield a **good operational decision**.

::: {.statement}
<p class="block-title">Central concern</p>
What happens between the LLM assessment and the operational outcome, and which configurations perform reliably?
:::

<p class="block-title">Experimental comparison</p>
Hold the **clinical-text inputs and patient groups fixed** when comparing how assessment configurations and decision policies interact. Vary operational settings deliberately and separately.
:::

## Main questions discussed

1. **Assessment accuracy:** How closely do LLM assessments agree with reference assessments?
2. **Operational performance:** Do more accurate assessments necessarily yield better allocations?
3. **Outcome robustness:** How do outcomes vary across optimal assignments, starting conditions, and client groups?
4. **Uncertainty-aware decisions:** What changes when LLM-reported probabilities enter a scenario-based decision model rather than a point-estimate model?
5. **Decision-aware inference (discussion direction):** Can an LLM's inference be partially or fully tailored to the downstream decision problem?

## Working example: pediatric rehabilitation caseload assignment {.compact}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="51%"}
::: {.statement}
<p class="block-title">Inputs</p>
- Pre-treatment notes (held fixed across compared models)
- Client complexity inferred from notes
- Existing clinician workloads
- Maximum number of clients per clinician and other feasibility restrictions
:::
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.statement}
<p class="block-title">Decision</p>
Assign incoming clients to clinicians to balance resulting **total complexity workload**, while respecting assignment and client-count restrictions.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.flow-summary}
Clinical text $\rightarrow$ complexity assessment $\rightarrow$ allocation $\rightarrow$ workload balance
:::

::: {.statement .scope}
<p class="block-title">Scope</p>
Caseload assignment is a working example for studying the text-to-decision pipeline, not evidence of clinical deployment effectiveness.
:::

## Assignment model: only the essential structure {.compact}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="51%"}
- $x_{ij}=1$ if client $i$ is assigned to clinician $j$.
- $s_i$: assessed client complexity.
- $H_j$: clinician $j$'s initial complexity load.
- Resulting load:

$$
W_j(x;s)=H_j+\sum_i s_i x_{ij}.
$$
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.statement}
<p class="block-title">Feasible assignments</p>
- Each incoming client is assigned once.
- Each clinician's allowed client count is respected.
- Other assignment restrictions remain the same across comparisons.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.statement}
<p class="block-title">Operational loss: complexity range</p>
$$
F(x;s,\theta)=\max_j W_j(x;s)-\min_j W_j(x;s).
$$
Here $\theta$ collects starting loads and constraints; lexicographic priorities, if present, are handled within each optimization model.
:::

## From LLM assessments to decision regret

- The decision system selects an allocation $x=D(\hat s;\theta)$ from LLM assessments $\hat s$.
- Evaluate $x$ using **reference assessments** $s^{\mathrm{ref}}$ under the **same** operational conditions.

$$
V^{\mathrm{ref}}(\theta)
=
\min_{y\in\mathcal X(\theta)}
F(y;s^{\mathrm{ref}},\theta)
$$

$$
\boxed{
R(x)=F(x;s^{\mathrm{ref}},\theta)-V^{\mathrm{ref}}(\theta)
}
$$

::: {.statement}
<p class="block-title">Interpretation</p>
Regret is the additional workload imbalance relative to the reference-information optimum. Reference labels evaluate the allocation; they do not generate the LLM-based decision.
:::

## Three distinct lenses on the same system

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="32%"}
::: {.statement}
<p class="block-title">Accuracy</p>
Agreement between LLM and reference labels.

Exact accuracy and quadratic-weighted $\kappa$.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="32%"}
::: {.statement}
<p class="block-title">Performance</p>
Cost of the resulting allocation.

Reference-evaluated regret and workload imbalance.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="32%"}
::: {.statement}
<p class="block-title">Robustness of outcomes</p>
**Distribution and variation** of regret and assignments across tested conditions.

Compare centers, spread, and outliers.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
**An accurate assessment need not yield a stable or high-performing decision.**
:::

## Where do differences in outcomes come from?

1. **Patient groups (chunks):** Different mixes of incoming clients.
2. **Starting clinician profiles:** Balanced, unbalanced, and highly unbalanced loads.
3. **Multiple optimal assignments:** Different allocations with equal modeled objective value, potentially different reference regret.

<!-- The iff?alse probability-distribution bullet in Slides.tex remains excluded. -->

::: {.statement}
<p class="block-title">Comparison principle</p>
Keep these sources separate where possible; a solver seed is not a probability scenario or an independently sampled patient population.
:::

## How LLM inference enters the decision model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.statement}
<p class="block-title">Deterministic input</p>
- LLM provides one complexity category per client.
- With class probabilities, select the **highest-probability class** (argmax).
- Optimize the assignment using these point assessments.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.statement}
<p class="block-title">Stochastic input</p>
- LLM reports probabilities for the complexity classes.
- Use those probabilities to generate possible complexity profiles.
- Choose **one allocation** with good average performance across sampled profiles.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.statement .scope}
<p class="block-title">Interpretation</p>
The difference lies in **how LLM inference is represented and used** by the downstream model, not in changing the original clinical notes.
:::

## A unified experimental design {.compact}

| Dimension | Design |
|:---|:---|
| LLM configuration | Qwen, MedGemma, and OpenDecider; compare prompting settings and self-reported confidence where available |
| Decision policy | Deterministic point-assessment versus scenario-based stochastic |
| Client composition | Common patient chunks for matched comparisons |
| Initial conditions | Balanced, unbalanced, highly unbalanced clinician loads; common count constraints |
| Solution selection | Different valid optimal assignments / solver selection seeds |
| Reference evaluation | **Proxy benchmark** used consistently to score regret; clinician labels where fully available |

::: {.takeaway}
**Analyze the resulting distributions of regret and assignments under comparable conditions.**
:::

## Conclusions

1. **Assessment--decision disconnect:** similar prediction quality, different regret.
2. **Context-dependent rankings:** different preferred LLM--decision combinations under different clinician loads.
3. **Solution-selection sensitivity:** identical modeled optimality, different reference outcomes.
4. **Uncertain inference:** when full class probabilities change allocation behavior compared with top-class labels.
5. **Decision-aware inference:** might information extraction itself be tailored to the downstream allocation task?

*These are questions for analysis, not established empirical findings.*
